A_target.statement:
Let $n$ objects be placed in $k$ boxes with $n > k$.
Then some box contains at least two objects.

B_source.statement:
Let $A, B$ be [[Definition:Finite Set|finite sets]] with $\card A > \card B$.
Then there is no [[Definition:Injection|injection]] $A \to B$.

substitutions.injectivity (no collisions): every box holds at most one item

derived.a collision: a box with two or more items

validity_conditions: An assignment with every box holding at most one item is precisely an injection from items to boxes.
With n items and k < n boxes, |items| > |boxes|, so no injection exists.
Failure of injectivity means some two items share a box - the pigeonhole conclusion.
proof_plan: View the placement as a [[Definition:Mapping|mapping]] $f$ from the set of $n$ objects to the set of $k$ boxes.
Every box holding at most one object means exactly that $f$ is [[Definition:Injection|injective]].
As $n > k$, by the source result there is no injection from objects to boxes.

Hence some box receives at least two objects, which is the [[Pigeonhole Principle]].
{{qed}}
